analysis.one_liner: Caps fees and interest on consumer credit—including payday, overdraft, and credit card loans—at 36%.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Banking Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Truth in Lending Act to make it illegal for any lender to charge consumers more than 36% a year in combined interest and fees—including payday loans, car title loans, bank overdraft fees, and credit card charges. It would count every fee toward that cap so lenders could not hide costs, require statements to show one true all-in rate labeled "FAIR," let state attorneys general sue violators, and impose prison time and fines on lenders who break the cap. Loans made in violation would be void, with all interest and fees returned to the borrower.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of Americans who use small-dollar credit: borrowers paying roughly 400% annual rates on payday loans, 300% on car title loans, triple-digit rates on online installment loans, and heavy overdraft fees on bank accounts would see those charges capped at 36% all-in, and loans made above the cap would be void with all money returned [S2][S3]. Servicemembers already have this cap under a 2006 law, and the bill's findings say that law curbed payday and title lending around military bases [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers using payday and overdraft credit

how_it_helps.text: No creditor could extend consumer credit where the combined fees and interest exceed 36%, closing loopholes that let payday lenders charge roughly 400% and bank overdraft fees reach effective rates near 17,000%.
Loans made above the cap are void: the borrower would get back all principal, interest, and fees, and violators face prison and fines up to triple the accrued debt or $50,000 per violation.
Credit card statements would show a single all-in 'FAIR' rate instead of an APR that hides fees, and state attorneys general could sue violators in federal court.

analysis.who_pays: Payday, car title, and online installment lenders would lose most of their business, since these loans are rarely profitable at 36% all-in; banks would lose overdraft and late-fee income; credit card issuers would have to cap rates and fees for the riskiest borrowers, likely cutting off some higher-risk customers from credit entirely rather than lending at a loss [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Consumers with poor or thin credit could lose access to emergency small-dollar credit entirely, since lenders may decline to serve them rather than lend at 36% or less, and no equivalent supply of cheaper loans is guaranteed to replace what disappears.

The bill applies a hard 36% ceiling to all consumer credit, including credit cards and installment loans, which lenders argue forces them to reprice or restrict accounts for riskier borrowers; the bill's own findings acknowledge high-cost lending fills a demand that would not simply vanish.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—ending triple-digit interest and fee stacking on small-dollar loans—is large for the people currently caught in those loans, and the military lending cap shows a 36% cap can work without credit vanishing. The cost is real and should be stated honestly: some higher-risk borrowers would lose access to emergency credit rather than get cheaper credit, and lenders would restrict who they serve. Tighter disclosure and tough enforcement strengthen the design, but the access question for thin-file borrowers remains the bill's main drawback.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Introduced September 6, 2023 by Senator Durbin, it was read twice and referred to the Banking Committee.
No further action was taken—no hearing, no markup, no vote—and the bill died at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.
It had only three cosponsors, all Democrats, so it never had the support to be scheduled on the Senate floor even if it had cleared committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday, title, and other high-cost lenders, plus banks earning overdraft and late-fee income, keep charging rates and fees that the cap would have banned.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-cost lenders and banks keep charging

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it to the Banking Committee.

for.name: Sens. Blumenthal, Merkley, and Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only three cosponsors it attracted.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill—no hearing, no markup, no vote—after it was referred on September 6, 2023.

against.name: Senate Republicans (41+ members)
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the bipartisan support typically needed to reach the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and all three cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-run Banking Committee never took the bill up.

industries.industry: Payday, car title, and high-cost installment lenders
industries.note: Their business model is lending at triple-digit rates; a national 36% all-in cap with criminal penalties and no exemptions would end most of it. Borrowers pay an average of ~400% on payday loans and ~300% on car title loans.

industries.industry: Banks and credit card issuers (overdraft and fee income)
industries.note: The bill counts overdraft, late, cash-advance, and over-limit fees toward the 36% cap, hitting the fee-heavy revenue banks earn from customers who carry balances or overdraw. Consumers currently pay tens of billions a year in overdraft and high-cost credit fees.

industries.industry: Credit card networks and issuers (interest revenue)
industries.note: Card issuers would face a hard ceiling on rates and stacked fees for subprime borrowers, but prime borrowers who pay low rates are largely untouched; lenders would likely tighten approvals for risky applicants.
